text: Arrays are useful because they summarize data quickly. NumPy gives you sum, mean, minimum, and maximum as one-line operations, either as methods on the array or as functions.

The new idea is the axis. Take a table of weekly sales, three stores in rows and four weeks in columns. Sum with no axis gives one grand total. Sum with axis zero gives a total for each week, and sum with axis one gives a total for each store. A simple way to remember it: the axis you name is the one that disappears.

Argmax gives the position of the largest value, and with an axis it returns one position per row or column. Without an axis, the position counts through the flattened array, so unravel index converts it back to a row and column.

Now center and spread. Suppose order values are twelve, fifteen, eleven, eighteen, fourteen, and ninety. The mean is about twenty-six point seven, pulled up by the ninety. The median is fourteen point five and barely notices it. When you suspect outliers, compare both.

Standard deviation measures spread, and here is a trap. NumPy divides by n by default, which is right when you have the whole population. For a sample, pass ddof equals one to divide by n minus one. Pandas uses ddof one by default, so results can differ between the two. Percentiles give the value below which a given share of the data falls. Percentile takes zero to one hundred, quantile takes zero to one.

To measure how two variables move together, corrcoef returns a matrix, and the off-diagonal entry is the correlation, between minus one and one. Missing values need care. A plain mean of an array containing nan returns nan, so use nanmean. And a z-score subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, using broadcasting, so each value shows how many standard deviations it sits from the mean.
You can now summarize data by axis and describe its center, spread, and relationships. Next lesson: random numbers and simulation.
